mappings.note: Gap-fill naming pi as the circumference-to-diameter ratio. C-7.3-LO-2's naming clause, not the irrationality outcome C-7.1-LO-3.
Heron's formula is the tool when the three SIDES are known and no height is available. C-5.1-LO-2's precondition; C-5.1-LO-1 is what to use when a height is given instead.
States Heron's formula and defines a, b, c and s. C-5.1-LO-2.
The 13-14-15 triangle worked through Heron with s = 21. Direct application of C-5.1-LO-2.
Both statements are about Heron's scope and about three sides determining a triangle -- the SSS fact that makes C-5.1-LO-2 work. Contrast qid:706790, where that condition fails for quadrilaterals.
Gap-fill for the semi-perimeter, the symbol most often mis-set in Heron's formula. C-5.1-LO-2.

The sides 40, 24, 32 satisfy 24^2+32^2 = 40^2, so the area can be found by Heron (LO-2) and again as half base times height using the two legs (LO-1). The item asks for both routes, so both are cited.
A 90 degree sector is a quarter of the circle's AREA. C-7.3-LO-4's extension from the circle to the sector.
Sector areas at equal angle scale as the SQUARE of the radius, because a sector is a fixed fraction of pi r squared. C-7.3-LO-4; the arc-length analogue would scale linearly.
Both quantities are asked for: the sector area, which is LO-4, and the arc length, which is LO-3. Keeping them apart is the point of the item.
A 120 degree sector is one third of the circle. Cited to LO-4 because the item is tagged and framed as sector area; the fraction is the step LO-4 rests on.
Runs the arc-length relation backwards to recover the angle from a 22 cm arc (LO-3), then uses that fraction for the area (LO-4). The inversion is what distinguishes it from qid:706780.
A median gives two triangles of equal area -- C-5.1-LO-4, stated as a fact.
The proof itself: equal bases from the midpoint and a shared perpendicular height. C-5.1-LO-4's 'proves that' clause.
All three medians drawn, with the six small triangles shown to be equal in area. C-5.1-LO-4 extended by repeated application, and a construction as well as a result.
22/7 is used because it is a convenient APPROXIMATION, not the value of pi. C-7.1-LO-3's 'why no fraction can give its exact value'.
An irrational times a non-zero whole number is irrational, so the circumference is never a whole number. A direct consequence of pi's irrationality, C-7.1-LO-3.
What irrationality means in practice -- non-terminating non-repeating expansion, and every used value being an approximation. C-7.1-LO-3 in full.
Brahmagupta's formula applies to a CYCLIC quadrilateral. C-5.1-LO-3's precondition.

Compares the two formulae and explains why four sides do not fix a quadrilateral without the cyclic condition, while three sides do fix a triangle. C-5.1-LO-3 is the comparison outcome and C-5.1-LO-2 the triangle half it is measured against.
A 60 degree arc is one sixth of the circumference. The angle-to-arc proportion that C-7.3-LO-3 is built on.
Derives arc length = theta/360 times 2 pi r, with a check at theta = 360. C-7.3-LO-3's 'calculates the length of an arc from its radius and central angle', here derived rather than applied.
Matches four central angles to their fractions of the circle -- the angle-to-fraction step of the arc-length outcome, C-7.3-LO-3.
Defines squaring a rectangle and names the required side as the geometric mean root(ab). C-7.1-LO-2.
Justifies why the side must be root(ab) and why that length is always constructible. C-7.1-LO-2's 'justifies each step' clause, argued rather than drawn.

The construction itself -- segments a and b in line, the semicircle on a+b as diameter, the perpendicular at their junction. C-7.1-LO-2 for the result, and C-7.4 because this item is the drawing task where qid:706795 is the argument.
